chapter_title: Introduction to Core Components: View, Text, Image
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of building user interfaces with React Native! At the heart of every React Native application are its core components, which serve as the building blocks for all visual elements. Unlike web development where you might use HTML tags like `
`, `

`, or ``, React Native provides its own set of components that map directly to native UI elements on iOS and Android. This ensures that your application looks and feels truly native on both platforms, rather than just being a web view wrapped in an app. Understanding these core components is absolutely crucial, as they form the foundation upon which all more complex UI elements are constructed. We'll start with three of the most fundamental: `View`, `Text`, and `Image`. The `View` component is arguably the most important and frequently used component in React Native. Think of it as the equivalent of a `

` in web development – a generic container that supports layout with Flexbox, styling, and touch handling. Every UI element you create, from simple buttons to complex navigation bars, will likely be nested within a `View`. It doesn't display anything on its own; instead, its primary purpose is to organize and structure other components. You'll use `View` components to group elements, apply padding or margins, set background colors, and define how its children are arranged using Flexbox. For instance, if you want to create a card-like UI element, you'd typically use a `View` as the card's container, then place `Text` and `Image` components inside it, all managed by the parent `View`'s layout properties. A common mistake beginners make is trying to apply styling directly to the root of a component without wrapping it in a `View`, which can lead to unexpected layout issues or errors. Always remember: `View` is your go-to for structural grouping and layout. Next, we have the `Text` component, which is specifically designed for displaying text. This might seem straightforward, but it's a critical distinction from web development. In React Native, you **must** wrap all textual content within a `Text` component. You cannot simply place a string of text directly inside a `View` or another component; doing so will result in an error. The `Text` component handles font rendering, text styling (like `fontSize`, `color`, `fontWeight`), and text-specific features such as `numberOfLines` for truncation. It also supports nesting other `Text` components to apply different styles to parts of a string, much like `` elements in HTML. For example, you could have a `Text` component containing "Hello, `World`!" to make "World" bold. This explicit requirement for `Text` components ensures consistent text rendering across different devices and operating systems. A common pitfall is forgetting to wrap text, especially when dealing with dynamic data. Always double-check that any string you intend to display is enclosed within `...`. Finally, the `Image` component allows you to display various types of images within your application. It's versatile, capable of rendering both local images (bundled with your app) and network images (fetched from a URL). For local images, you use the `require()` function within the `source` prop, like `source={require('./assets/my-image.png')}`. This tells React Native to bundle the image with your application. For network images, the `source` prop expects an object with a `uri` key, like `source={{ uri: 'https://example.com/logo.png' }}`. It's crucial to remember that network images often require specific dimensions (width and height) to be applied via the `style` prop, otherwise they might not appear because their intrinsic size is unknown until loaded. Local images, on the other hand, can often infer their dimensions, but explicitly setting them is still good practice for consistent layout. The `Image` component also supports various `resizeMode` properties (e.g., `cover`, `contain`, `stretch`) to control how the image scales within its bounds. A safety note here: when loading network images, always consider potential network issues or slow loading times. You might want to implement a loading indicator or placeholder image to improve the user experience. Additionally, ensure your image assets are appropriately sized and optimized to prevent excessive memory usage and slow performance, especially on older devices. These three components—`View`, `Text`, and `Image`—are the bedrock of any React Native UI. By mastering their individual roles and how they interact, you'll be well on your way to building engaging and robust cross-platform applications. Remember to always consider the native context: `View` for containers, `Text` for all text, and `Image` for all visuals, each with their specific requirements and best practices.

screens.title: Introduction to Core Components: View, Text, Image
screens.subtitle: Learn the building blocks that map to native UI: containers, text rendering, and images.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn three fundamental React Native components that form every UI: the View container, the Text renderer, and the Image visual. These components map directly to native widgets on iOS and Android, which means your app feels like a native app rather than a wrapped web page. You'll see how View organizes layout with Flexbox, why all textual content must live inside Text components, and how Image handles both bundled and network pictures along with the practical requirement to size them. We'll also explore common mistakes you might make as a beginner — like placing raw strings inside a View or forgetting to give a network image explicit dimensions — and how to fix them quickly. A hands-on activity will guide you through building a simple profile card that uses all three components. By the end, you'll understand not only syntax but the why: why React Native separates text and visual primitives, and why layout and sizing decisions matter for cross-platform performance and appearance. Think about a simple app screen you use daily; these three components are what make that screen possible. What native behaviors do you expect when you open that app?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Master View for structure, Text for any text content, and Image for visuals; together they form the native UI foundation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify React Native's core UI primitives, use View to structure layouts, render text correctly with Text, and load images with the Image component. First, you'll recognize when to pick a View as a container and how Flexbox powers layout decisions. Second, you'll be able to wrap any textual content in a Text component, nest Text fragments for inline styling, and use the number-of-lines property to truncate long strings. Third, you'll distinguish between local and network images, use require for bundled assets, and apply explicit width and height for network images so they display consistently. Finally, you'll spot common beginner errors — such as unwrapped strings or missing image dimensions — and know how to fix them quickly. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue so you remember which primitive to use and why. These objectives map directly to the ProfileCard activity where you'll put all of these skills together and verify your competency by rendering an avatar, name, and bio with correct layout and sizing. Think of these objectives as checkboxes you can test by running the starter code and confirming the UI renders without errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Skills to practice and common beginner mistakes to avoid

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and common pitfalls you will intentionally avoid. You'll practice a small ProfileCard task: set up a View container, include an Image for the avatar, and place two Text elements for name and bio. While coding, verify that text is wrapped in Text components and that any externally loaded image has explicit width and height. A key misconception is thinking text can be placed directly inside View; that leads to a render error. Another common oversight is assuming network images will size themselves; without explicit dimensions they may not appear. Practicing these checks will save you time when debugging. We'll also discuss how styling is applied through the style prop and how arrays of style objects merge, which helps when composing reusable style objects. Finally, you'll learn a quick debugging checklist: check imports, ensure Text wraps strings, give network images sizes, and confirm require paths for local assets. Practicing with these focused steps will make layout issues less mysterious and help you build predictable native-feeling screens faster.

screens.title: Why React Native uses its own primitives
screens.subtitle: Understanding the mapping to native widgets

narration.text: React Native provides its own UI primitives so components render as native platform widgets instead of a web view. That means when you use a View, Text, or Image, React Native translates them into the closest native element on iOS and Android. The practical result is better platform fidelity and performance. If you've done web work, you might expect div, p, and img to behave the same, but React Native intentionally separates these roles. For example, Text handles font rendering and line metrics consistently across devices; Image integrates with native image pipelines and memory constraints; View manages touch and layout in a platform-aware way. A common beginner misconception is to treat these as simple aliases for web tags; they are not. Another example: styling and layout are applied via the style prop and Flexbox, but underlying rendering and available properties differ because each primitive maps to native capabilities. Understanding this mapping helps you predict behavior — for instance, why nested Text elements allow inline formatting, or why Image may require explicit sizing for network resources. Reflect on a mobile screen you use daily: its smooth scrolling and native typography are the direct result of these native mappings. How does thinking in native terms change how you design your UI components?

keyIdea.title: Mapping matters
keyIdea.text: View, Text, and Image map to native widgets so your app behaves and performs like a real native app.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Native Mapping
Definition

React Native primitives are lightweight wrappers that instruct the native renderer to create corresponding platform widgets. This ensures UI fidelity, native performance, and consistent behavior across devices.

Analogy

Think of View, Text, and Image as instructions to a native UI factory. You specify structure and properties; the factory creates the actual native parts.

Misconception

These components are not direct copies of web tags — they map to native controls and may expose platform-specific behaviors.

Concrete examples
  • Text: Handles font metrics and inline nesting for mixed styles.
  • Image: Uses native image loading; network images often need width and height.
  • View: Manages layout, background, and touch interaction like a native container.
Key Takeaway

Design for native behavior: think in components that the platform will actually render.

screens.title: Using View for layout and grouping
screens.subtitle: How to structure UI using View and Flexbox

narration.text: View is the primary building block for layout in React Native — it acts as a container for other components and supports styling and Flexbox-based positioning. Start by thinking of View as a box that can hold children. Use the style prop to set padding, margin, background color, border radius, and Flexbox properties such as flex-direction, justify-content, and align-items. A typical pattern is a parent View with flex-direction set to row for horizontal layout or column for vertical stacking, and child Views with flex values to control proportional sizing. A common beginner error is trying to style text outside of Text components or assuming default spacing will match web defaults. Another frequent oversight is forgetting to set min-height or explicit flex values when a container must fill available space. When grouping UI, keep styles modular: extract shared container styles and compose them with arrays of style objects so you can layer base layout and overrides. For practical setup, structure a card View, then inside it place an Image followed by a nested View for two Text lines. This predictable grouping simplifies alignment and makes responsive adjustments easier. As you practice, ask yourself whether a piece of UI is structural or representational — if it's structural, wrap it in a View.

keyIdea.title: View is layout
keyIdea.text: Use View to group and position content using Flexbox, padding, and composable styles.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › View Layout
Layout pattern

Typical process to structure a card UI:

  1. Create a parent View as card container and set padding and borderRadius.
  2. Place an Image or avatar inside a child View and give it fixed size.
  3. Use a nested View for Text lines and control spacing with margin and align-items.
Pro tip

Compose styles with arrays so you can reuse a base container and add modifiers on demand.

Visual example
Parent View
Child View
Nested View
This grouping makes it easy to set flex behavior on the parent and fine-tune children without surprise overrides.
Key Takeaway

Use View for structure and rely on Flexbox properties to control layout across devices.

screens.title: Text component: rules and nesting
screens.subtitle: Why every string must be in Text and how to style fragments

narration.text: Text is the only component designed to render textual content in React Native. Unlike the web where you might place raw strings inside containers, React Native enforces that all text be wrapped in a Text component. This ensures consistent font measurement, line height, and platform-specific text handling. You can also nest Text components to apply different styles to inline fragments; for example, a bold word within a sentence can be another Text with a bold style. Text supports several useful props: font styling via style, and number-of-lines to truncate content to a set number of lines with an ellipsis. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to import Text from React Native, which yields a runtime error when a string appears in a View. Another subtle issue is assuming text inherits styles from parent Views — it does not. Use style objects or arrays of styles with Text to compose fontSize, color, and weight. A concrete example: displaying a username and bio requires two Text elements so you can set different font sizes and truncate the bio without affecting the username. Finally, when working with dynamic data, always guard that the value is a string or render a fallback Text to avoid rendering undefined values.

keyIdea.title: Text rules
keyIdea.text: Wrap all text in Text components, nest for inline styles, and use number-of-lines to control truncation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Text Rules
Definition & behavior

Text is responsible for font rendering, line height, and inline nesting. Always import and wrap strings to avoid render errors.

Example

Use two Text components: one for a bold name and another for a truncated bio using number-of-lines.

Common mistake

Placing a raw string inside a View triggers an error; always wrap it in Text.

Nesting & styles
<Text>Hello, <Text style={{fontWeight: 'bold'}}>World</Text>!</Text>

Use nesting to style inline fragments without splitting layout into separate lines.

Key Takeaway

Treat Text as the canonical container for any rendered string and style fragments by nesting Text elements.

screens.title: Image: local vs network and the source prop
screens.subtitle: How to provide images and why dimensions matter

narration.text: The Image component displays visuals and supports both local assets and network resources. Local images are included in your app bundle and are referenced using require with a file path. Network images use an object with a uri property. A crucial practical difference is that network images often need explicit width and height via the style prop; without these values a network image may not appear because its intrinsic size is unknown until loaded. Local images can often infer dimensions, but it's still good practice to set sizes for consistent layout. Another important prop is resizeMode which controls how the image scales inside its bounding box with options like cover, contain, and stretch. Beginners sometimes assume Image will automatically scale to fit a container; instead, choose a resizeMode that matches your design intent and provide explicit size constraints. Also consider memory and performance: large images increase memory usage on device, so optimize assets and prefer appropriately sized images for mobile. For a concrete example, use require for an avatar bundled with your app or an external URL for a profile picture, and always set width and height to avoid invisible or mis-sized images.

keyIdea.title: Image source
keyIdea.text: Use require for local assets, {uri: '...'} for network images, and set explicit dimensions for reliable rendering.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Image Source
Source patterns
// Local image
source = require('./assets/avatar.png')

// Network image
source = { uri: 'https://example.com/avatar.png' }

Local images are bundled and referenced with require. Network images use a uri object and typically need width and height defined.

Resize modes

cover, contain, and stretch change how the image fits its box. Pick one to preserve aspect ratio or to fill the container.

Concrete example
A profile avatar from the network should use a fixed width and height and resizeMode set to cover so the image fills the circular frame without distortion.
Key Takeaway

Always provide dimensions for network images and choose a resize mode that matches your visual intent.

screens.title: Local images vs Network images
screens.subtitle: Differences in bundling, sizing, and behavior

narration.text: Local and network images behave differently and you should pick the right approach depending on the use case. Local images are bundled with the app using require and are included at build time. They often expose intrinsic dimensions and load immediately from the device storage. This makes them ideal for small icons or assets that must be available offline. Network images are fetched at runtime using a uri and depend on the user's connection and server latency. Because React Native cannot know a network image's dimensions before it loads, you must set explicit width and height in the style or the image may not render. Another important contrast is update behavior: changing a local image requires a new app build, while network images can update without redeploying the app. For example, for a static logo bundled with the app, use a local asset. For user avatars that can change, use a network uri and consider showing a placeholder while the image loads. Common mistakes include forgetting to style network images and assuming require paths will resolve for remote files. Choosing the correct source pattern and handling loading states will make your UI robust and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Choose source carefully
keyIdea.text: Use local assets for static graphics and network images for dynamic content; always size network images and handle loading states.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Image Comparison
Local images
  • Bundled at build time using require.
  • Often have intrinsic dimensions and load instantly.
  • Best for app icons and fixed assets.
Note

Changing a local image requires a new app build and redeploy.

Network images
  • Retrieved at runtime via a uri object.
  • Require explicit width and height for reliable rendering.
  • Good for dynamic user content like avatars.
Pro tip

Show a placeholder while network images load to improve perceived performance.

screens.title: Hands-on: ProfileCard starter template
screens.subtitle: Walk through the starter code and required styles

narration.text: Let's walk through the starter template for the ProfileCard component step by step. The component imports View, Text, Image, and StyleSheet from React Native. The top-level View acts as the card container where you apply background color, padding, and border radius. Inside, the Image represents the avatar; for a network avatar you must include width and height and likely use resizeMode set to cover for a circular crop. Beneath the avatar, use a Text for the user's name with a larger fontSize and fontWeight, and another Text for the bio which can use number-of-lines to truncate. A beginner mistake is leaving out Text imports or using a raw string. Another common error is omitting styles for network images so they do not render. When you set styles, prefer creating a StyleSheet object and pass styles via the style prop; you can also pass an array to combine base and override styles. In the activity, implement TODOs for the Image source, Text content, and styles. After implementing, run the app and verify the avatar appears, the name is bold, and the bio truncates if it is long. This hands-on loop will cement how View, Text, and Image work together in a real component.

keyIdea.text: Implement the ProfileCard by setting Image source and sizing, wrapping strings in Text, and composing styles with StyleSheet.

Fill the TODOs: set avatar source and size, wrap text with Text, and style the container for padding and background.

screens.title: Fixing a common error: raw strings inside View
screens.subtitle: Diagnose and correct the 'raw string' render error

narration.text: A very common error for beginners is placing a raw string inside a View without wrapping it in a Text component. This triggers a render-time error because React Native requires textual content to be explicitly wrapped. Let's diagnose and fix the issue. Imagine the component returns a View with the string Hello World and an Image. The error message often points to a text node in a place where a component was expected. The fix is simple: import Text from react-native and wrap the string in a Text element. While making the change, remember to style Text for fontSize and color separately from View. Another subtle source of the issue is forgetting to include Text in the import list; this yields a different but related runtime complaint. After applying the fix, rebuild the app and confirm the string renders. Also, check that any dynamic values you render are strings or converted to strings, otherwise null or undefined may produce unexpected layouts. This debugging exercise reinforces two rules: always wrap rendered strings in Text, and verify component imports before assuming the runtime bug is more complex.

keyIdea.title: Debug rule
keyIdea.text: If you see a render error caused by a text node, ensure all strings are wrapped with Text and Text is imported.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Debugging Text
Problem scenario
// Incorrect
<View>
  Hello World!
  <Image source={{ uri: 'https://example.com/logo.png' }} />
</View>

The raw string causes a render error because it is not wrapped by a Text component.

Fix

Wrap the string with Text and ensure Text is imported from react-native.

Corrected example
// Correct
import { View, Text, Image } from 'react-native';

<View>
  <Text>Hello World!</Text>
  <Image source={{ uri: 'https://example.com/logo.png' }} style={{ width: 100, height: 100 }} />
</View>
Key Takeaway

Simple fixes — wrap strings and provide image sizes — solve many beginner render issues quickly.

screens.title: Image resizeMode and presentation
screens.subtitle: How cover, contain, and stretch affect visuals

narration.text: Image resizeMode controls how an image fits its bounding box. The three common values are cover, contain, and stretch. Cover scales the image to fill the box while preserving aspect ratio; parts may be clipped if the aspect ratios differ. Contain scales the image to fit entirely inside the box, preserving aspect ratio but possibly leaving empty space. Stretch distorts the image to fill the box exactly, ignoring aspect ratio. Choosing the right mode depends on the visual goal: use cover when you want a cropped, edge-to-edge avatar or hero image; use contain when you must show the entire image without cropping; and use stretch only when distortion is acceptable or the asset is designed for resizing. A practical example: for avatars use cover with fixed width and height and a circular borderRadius so images fill the circle, but for logos that must remain undistorted use contain with padding. Remember that resizeMode interacts with layout: if you don't set explicit dimensions, network images may remain invisible regardless of resizeMode. Always combine the chosen resizeMode with appropriate width, height, and borderRadius to create predictable visuals across devices.

keyIdea.title: resizeMode rule
keyIdea.text: Pick cover to fill and crop, contain to fit without cropping, and avoid stretch unless distortion is acceptable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › resizeMode
Modes explained
  • cover: fills box and preserves aspect ratio, may crop edges.
  • contain: fits entire image inside box, may leave empty space.
  • stretch: forces image to fill box, may distort.
Example

Use cover for avatar circles and hero images; use contain for logos that must not be cropped.

Visual test cases
Avatar with cover
Logo with contain
Banner with stretch

These quick choices determine whether your image will crop, letterbox, or distort inside its frame.

Key Takeaway

Pair your chosen resizeMode with explicit sizing to ensure predictable rendering across devices.

narration.text: Now apply what you've learned in a hands-on activity: build the ProfileCard that displays an avatar, a name, and a short bio. Follow this checklist. First, create a functional component that returns a View as the container and style it with background color, padding, and borderRadius. Second, add an Image for the avatar; if you use a network uri, set width and height (for example 80 by 80) and choose resizeMode cover. Third, add a Text for the name, style it to be bold and larger, and add another Text for the bio with number-of-lines set to 2 to truncate long bios. Fourth, compose styles with StyleSheet. create and pass arrays if you need to combine base and override styles. Finally, test the component: confirm there are no render errors, the avatar appears, the name is bold, and the bio truncates as expected. A common check is to verify imports include View, Text, Image, and StyleSheet. If the avatar is missing, double-check the uri or require path and the width/height values. This activity reinforces the complete flow: structure with View, text with Text, and visuals with Image — the exact primitives that power most mobile screens.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Deliver a working ProfileCard with correct imports, wrapped text, sized image, and composed styles.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › ProfileCard Activity
Implementation checklist
  1. Create View container with padding and background.
  2. Add Image for avatar with width, height, and resizeMode.
  3. Add Text for name and Text for bio with number-of-lines.
  4. Compose and apply styles via StyleSheet.create.
Testing steps

Run the app, check for render errors, verify the avatar loads, the name is bold, and the bio truncates when long.

Example expectations

Name: larger font-size, bold

Follow the checklist and the ProfileCard will demonstrate correct use of View, Text, and Image together.

screens.title: Performance and UX considerations for images
screens.subtitle: Avoiding large assets and handling loading states

narration.text: Images can be a leading source of performance problems on mobile. Large uncompressed images increase memory usage and slow rendering, especially on older devices. To avoid this, use appropriately sized images for the display density you target and prefer compressed formats. For network images, implement a loading placeholder or skeleton to give users immediate feedback while the image downloads. A simple pattern is to render a local placeholder image or a colored View with a spinner until the network image reports loaded. Another consideration is cache behavior: network images may be cached by the native layer, but caching strategies vary across platforms and servers. For avatars and small images, prefer smaller dimensions and consider server-side resizing to match frontend requirements. Finally, be mindful of resizeMode and scaling; forcing stretch or large upscaling will produce poor visual quality and more memory pressure. In practice, test on lower-end devices and on slow network conditions to observe the real user experience. These steps make your app feel faster and more reliable — and they prevent crashes caused by excessive memory consumption. Performance and UX considerations for images means optimize image sizes, show placeholders while loading, and test on low-end devices to ensure good ux and memory use.. In practical terms, avoiding large assets and handling loading states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Image performance
keyIdea.text: Optimize image sizes, show placeholders while loading, and test on low-end devices to ensure good UX and memory use.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Image Performance
Performance checklist
  • Use appropriately sized images and compress assets.
  • Show placeholders or skeletons while network images load.
  • Prefer server-side resizing for dynamic images when possible.
Testing

Test on slower networks and lower-end devices to surface memory and loading issues early.

UX patterns

Placeholder example: render a circular View with a background color until the avatar finishes loading, then fade in the Image. This keeps layout stable and reduces perceived loading time.

Key Takeaway

Small images and placeholders dramatically improve perceived performance and avoid memory spikes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember about View, Text, and Image

narration.text: Let's restate the core ideas you should carry forward. First: View is the structural container; use it for grouping, layout with Flexbox, and applying spacing and background. Second: Text is the only valid container for strings; always wrap textual content in Text and use nested Text elements for inline styling and truncation via number-of-lines. Third: Image displays visuals and supports local assets via require and network images via a uri object; network images typically need explicit width and height and an appropriate resize mode. Also remember practical checks: verify imports, size network images, use placeholders while loading, and optimize image assets for memory and performance. These concepts together form the foundation of nearly every screen you will build in React Native. Keep this checklist handy when you start new components: choose View for structure, Text for strings, and Image for pictures. With these rules, your UIs will be predictable, native-feeling, and easier to debug.

keyIdea.text: View = structure, Text = all strings, Image = visuals with explicit sizing for network sources.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Concepts
View

A container for layout and grouping that uses Flexbox and style for spacing and background.

Text

All textual content must be inside Text. Use nesting for inline styles and number-of-lines to truncate long strings.

Image

Displays local or network images via source. Network images usually need explicit width and height and a suitable resizeMode.

Summary

Apply the simple rules: View for structure, Text for all strings, Image for visuals with correct sizing and handling for network assets.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick recall cards for practice and debugging

narration.text: To close, keep these three recall checks in your toolkit. First, always wrap strings in Text and import Text from React Native. Second, size network images explicitly and choose the correct resize mode to avoid invisible or distorted images. Third, use View to structure layout with Flexbox and compose styles with StyleSheet so your design is modular and maintainable. When debugging, run a small checklist: imports, Text wrappers, image dimensions, and require paths. Use the ProfileCard activity to practice these checks until they become second nature. These rules will significantly reduce the most common beginner errors and speed up your development workflow. Which one will you check first the next time a component doesn't render as expected? keyIdea.text: Wrap text, size images, and structure with View — run the checklist when debugging.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Quick Recall
Check text

Import and use Text for any string to avoid render errors.

Check images

For network images, set width and height and pick a suitable resizeMode.

Check layout

Use View with Flexbox and compose styles for predictable layout behavior.

Final take

These three checks will quickly point you to the most common reasons a UI fails to render correctly.
